title: St. Louis: Fate Marable, Charlie Creath, George Hudson and a Kenton jam
summary: Moore recalls St. Louis bandleaders and a jam session with Clark Terry and Vido Musso.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Working the Streckfus riverboats with Fate Marable

blocks.x: Well, Jeter-Pillars had some good but it was also great. Had some good arrangers in St. Louis. arrangements there, Another fella used to come around there was Fate Marable.
An old man from New Orleans.
Whenever he was in town, he always came to the club to hear our band.
You didn't meet him in New Orleans when

No, I didn't, I was in St. Louis when I met Fate Marable. I can't recall the famous names but I remember Fate, but that was a big name then. Louis was with him.

There was a man there called Charlie Creath and Charlie Creath is the brother to the wife of Zutty Singleton -- Marge. And his claim to fame, Charlie Creath. And I don't know too much about them, I think some of these days I'd like to get in touch with Marge -- Zutty passed away, and I know Marge was telling me all about her brother, Charlie Creath. I met him in St. Louis. I didn't hear the band he had but he had a band and a great band at that, you know. There was another band called George Hudson
Okay, George Hudson, who did he have in his band?

The most famous. I can think of is Clark Terry. Even then he was a beautiful, great trumpet player. One night Sam Kenton came by, played an engagement and out of that Sam Kenton band some of the guys from the band came out to sit in in one of

the spots in St. Louis and one I remember was Vido Musso myself, and some of the guys from Harlan Leonard's band was there, and Clark Terry. I keep thinking about -- the names go by so fast.
Clark Terry, you were impressed with his playing at that time?

Vido Musso has been around with a number of orchestras and so in the St. Louis area he was a fixture on the scene or at least he would pass through a lot at that time? He came out of California, didn't he?
Yeah, he was with Stan Kenton.

It was a beautiful jam session. To hear those guys blow -- wonderful, inspiring, makes you want to blow just as well as they used to blow. We all tried to copy each other, head-cutting, you know. We called that we used to have in New Orleans, that head-cutting sessions, you know.
